lesson.title: Bill Clinton and the Age of Globalization
lesson.summary: Bill Clinton's presidency from 1993 to 2001 coincided with the end of the Cold War and a historic wave of economic globalization that reshaped American prosperity, politics, and America's place in the world.
lesson.body:
Bill Clinton won the presidency in 1992 by focusing relentlessly on the economy, which had slipped into recession under George H.W. Bush. Clinton took office at a hinge moment in world history. The Soviet Union had dissolved in December 1991, ending more than four decades of Cold War competition and leaving the United States as the world's only superpower. Without a rival superpower to contain, American policy makers began redirecting attention and resources, sometimes called a peace dividend, from military spending toward economic competitiveness.

Clinton embraced globalization, the accelerating flow of goods, capital, and information across national borders, as the defining economic force of the decade. His administration pushed through the North American Free Trade Agreement, helped bring the World Trade Organization into existence in 1995, and later granted China permanent normal trade relations, all bets that opening markets would grow the American economy even as it exposed American workers to new competition. At the same time, a boom in personal computing and the early internet, along with low inflation and low unemployment, produced one of the longest peacetime economic expansions in American history to that point, culminating in federal budget surpluses by the late 1990s, the first in decades.

Domestically, Clinton governed as a self described New Democrat, moving his party toward the political center through a strategy his advisors called triangulation, positioning himself between liberal Democrats and the conservative Republican Congress elected in 1994. This approach produced the 1996 welfare reform law and a balanced budget, but also drew criticism from the left for cutting the social safety net and from the right for a lack of consistent conviction. Clinton's presidency was also marked by scandal and impeachment in 1998 and 1999 over the Monica Lewinsky affair, though the Senate acquitted him and he remained popular through his final year in office.

Abroad, without the organizing logic of Cold War containment, Clinton faced a world of scattered regional conflicts and humanitarian crises, from failed intervention in Somalia in 1993 to NATO led action in Bosnia and later in Kosovo. His presidency set the template that later administrations would build on and react against: an America deeply enmeshed in global trade and finance, confident in its unmatched power, and only beginning to grapple with the risks that interconnected markets and open borders could also bring.
